results.title: Bride of Chucky
results.creator_credit: Ronny Yu, David Kirschner, Grace Gilroy and Universal Pictures
results.brief_description: This is the fourth, and without a doubt the best in the controversial ‘Child’s play’ series. In the latest instalment Chucky (voiced supplied by Brad Dourif), the benevolent child’s toy is bought back to life in this inventive and witty sequel which plays more like a demented homage to ‘Bride of Frankenstein’. The sinister looking doll which is possessed by the evil spirit of a serial killer is resurrected from the dead by his unbalanced goth girlfriend (played with relish by Jennifer Tilly), who has wedding bells on her mind. However Chucky has more sinister intentions than marriage, when he and his trailer trash bride stow away with two runaway teens wrongly accused of murder. Hong Kong director Ronny Yu (‘Bride with the white hair’), and writer Don Mancini have fashioned a wonderfully irresponsible film which proudly wears it’s horror film references on its sleeve, giving the series some surreal, clever twists and turns. Cast also includes John Ritter, Alexis Arquette and Katherine Heigl.

results.title: Thunderbirds are go
results.creator_credit: David Lane, Sylvia Anderson and Associated Television (Overseas) Ltd
results.brief_description: The Tracy team launch a highly dangerous rescue mission in space in this first feature-length Thunderbirds classic. SZero X, a 21st century spacecraft, is suddenly blasted by a strange explosion as it leaves the Earth’s atmosphere bound for Mars. Is it sabotage? Can the Thunderbirds discover the perpetrators and save the next launch? This adventure film is gadget loaded and features visual effects by Derek Meddings as well as sound effects by some of London’s famous rock stars, including Cliff Richards.

results.title: The Great Muppet caper
results.creator_credit: Jim Henson, David Lazer, Frank Oz and ITC Entertainment
results.brief_description: Kermit and Fozzie Bear star as twin reporters, who together with the rest of the Muppet gang travel to Great Britain in search of jewel thieves. Catching the guilty culprits seems to be the only action to redeem themselves with their boss for letting the thieves escape under their very noses. During their stay Kermit meets Miss Piggy posing as fashion designer Lady Holiday (Diana Rigg), the woman whose gems have been stolen. While the Muppets are in Britain another of Lady Holiday’s diamonds is stolen and Miss Piggy is arrested on suspicion of theft. Now there is even more at stake than their jobs as the Muppets race to clear Miss Piggy’s name and stop another theft from occurring. Features cameos by Peter Falk, John Cleese, Peter Ustinov and others.

results.title: The Gold Rush (1925)
results.brief_description: The Gold Rush, an immortal classic, is regarded as one of Chaplin’s very best films, interweaving to brilliant effect the pathetic tale of the Tramp’s apparently hopeless love for a dancehall girl with the funny story of the Tramp and his burly gold prospecting partner heading off to make their fortunes in the great Yukon gold rush. Through the entire film hangs Chaplin’s finely perceived view of the contrast between the Tramp’s selfless, humanitarian behaviour, and the unpleasant, brutish life of the gold town society. Rated: G

results.creator_credit: Guy Baskin, Shepherd Baker Studios and Woodside Petroleum Ltd
results.brief_description: Depicts the final stages of construction, as well as the tow, launch and placement of the substructure for the first offshore production platform for the North West Shelf Project. results.title: Yoda puppetry components
results.credit_line: Courtesy, Nick Maley, Yoda Guy Movie Museum
results.brief_description:
Iconic, Yoda is. Small, funny and wise, he changed what a screen hero, or Jedi, could be. First appeared he did in Star Wars: Episode V – The Empire Strikes Back (1980), beloved through Frank Oz’s expressive performance.

Since then, in many forms Yoda has appeared: different puppets, a CGI character and, in Star Wars: The Last Jedi (2017), a version closer to his original puppet self. Strong with this one, the puppet is.

Designing Yoda

Yoda began with a simple brief: he needed to look very old, wise and not quite human. Early sketches made him more animal-like, but the design gradually settled on smaller, wrinkled and gnome-like. These drawings gave sculptors a starting point, but Yoda’s personality emerged through modelling, texture and masterful puppeteering. 

Head of make-up and creature effects Stuart Freeborn spent five months sculpting Yoda’s face. A photograph of Albert Einstein in the workshop inspired some of the wrinkles around Yoda’s eyes, though the final character also looked a lot like Freeborn himself. Yoda’s size was shaped around the length and width of puppeteer Frank Oz’s arm, so that Oz could perform the Jedi master from inside. David Barclay also joined Freeborn’s team, helping build Yoda before becoming one of his puppeteers.

Performing Yoda

Yoda’s power may come from the Force, but his character comes through performance. Frank Oz performed Yoda’s voice and main puppetry, bringing the wisdom, humour and impatience of the little Jedi master to life. David Barclay initially operated Yoda’s eyes, while other puppeteers controlled his ears and right hand. The ears were especially expressive, moved by cables that let them lift, droop or sharpen Yoda’s reactions.

Four Yoda puppets were made for Star Wars: Episode V – The Empire Strikes Back (1980). Nick Maley worked on all four, including a back-up puppet that ended up being used for most of Yoda’s scenes after the primary model often malfunctioned.  When Oz became unavailable for the final week of filming, he chose Barclay to take over Yoda’s main puppetry.

Rebuilding Yoda 

Decades after Star Wars: Episode V – The Empire Strikes Back (1980), Nick Maley returned to one of the puppets that defined his career. In 2016, he began reverse engineering a faithful rebuild of the back-up Yoda puppet he had helped create in 1979. The rebuild was completed in 2021. 

Maley now takes the rebuilt Yoda to speaking events, Comic Cons, schools and children’s hospitals, using the puppet to inspire new generations of makers, fans and storytellers. The project shows how screen puppetry depends on specialised craft that can easily be lost if it isn’t preserved and shared.

results.title: Digital Puppetry: Video Essay
results.brief_description:
Digital puppetry uses pixels as the puppet’s body. Instead of strings, rods or hands inside the puppet, movement can be captured through motion-capture suits, facial cameras, sensors and tracking markers. Animators then work with digital rigs to shape the final character on screen.

The tools have changed, but the relationship is familiar. Someone still guides another body, helping it move, react and seem alive.

results.title: Special effects in Blade Runner (Spinners)
results.brief_description: Blade runner Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford) hunts rogue replicants through the rain-drenched, neon-lit streets of a futuristic Los Angeles in Ridley Scott’s groundbreaking Blade Runner (1982).

constellations_primary.name: The Kubrick connection
constellations_primary.description: The visual effects for Blade Runner drew on a number of techniques from other iconic films, including two of Stanley Kubrick's masterpieces.

results.description:
Blade runner Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford) hunts rogue replicants through the rain-drenched, neon-lit streets of a futuristic Los Angeles in Ridley Scott’s groundbreaking Blade Runner (1982).   

Aside from the influential dystopian setting, Blade Runner is lauded for its striking visual effects, particularly the ‘spinners’ – hi-tech cars that soar through the streets and the sky. Scott was inspired by imagery in several of these books. Futurist and industrial designer Syd Mead also contributed, helping design the sci-fi world around the cars.   

Spinner models were filmed against a black screen and then superimposed on the model shots of LA. Three life-size versions of the spinners were also created. These flew on wires that were later painted out of the shots, while interior shots were filmed against a green screen.

results.title: Biscuits by the million
results.creator_credit: Roy A. Driver and Herschells Films
results.brief_description: This is story of biscuit manufacture in a modern factory of the 50’s. The flour, sugar and milk that forms the basic dough of every biscuit is mixed, kneaded, rolled, stretched and stamped, and ready for final baking in a long oven through which biscuits pass continuously. When cooled they are packed in tins, the only operation carried out by hand. Most of the biscuits are consumed locally, although a percentage are exported to other parts of the world.
